title: SIEM export operational notes and customer templates
content:
Purpose and scope:

This note is an operational-focused companion for SIEM exports covering customer requirements, field-mapping templates, and practical runbook steps for Splunk HEC, Datadog Logs API, and Azure Sentinel (Log Analytics). It also covers integration considerations with RBAC v2, the audit-log schema we emit, and how evidence-automation hooks into the export pipeline.

Intended audience:
- Security engineers at customer orgs and Redwoods' integration engineers
- Solutions engineering and CSM when scoping enterprise onboarding
- SRE/Platform for monitoring connector health

High-level export modes we support (summary):
1) Push over HTTPS (preferred) - NDJSON batches to HEC / Datadog / Sentinel collector endpoint. TLS 1.2+, mTLS optional.
2) Syslog (less common) - RFC5424 formatted over TLS to customer syslog collectors. Useful for air-gapped proxies.
3) SFTP drop - batched compressed files (gzip) for customers requiring offline ingestion.

Key customer requirement patterns seen in trials:
- Centralized tenant-level logging: customers want a single dataset per tenant or workspace, with tenant_id present in every event.
- Immutable audit trail: retention plus tamper-evidence using event checksums and sequence ids.
- Minimal PII leakage: masks for email/phone in request/response payloads before export.
- Real-time vs batched: security teams need near real-time alerts; compliance teams accept hourly batches.
- RBAC alignment: map our internal role names to customer's identity/principal fields so alerts can tie back to actual user identities.

Audit log schema (recommended canonical fields) - we emit these keys; connectors should map them 1:1 when possible:
- timestamp: ISO8601 UTC (string)
- event_type: short tag (e.g., "session.create", "model.invoke", "policy.change")
- request_id: opaque UUID (string)
- tenant_id: customer org id (string)
- principal_type: user|service_account|api_key
- principal_id: user id or service account id
- principal_name: display name or email (subject to PII masking policy)
- resource_type: model|route|dataset|key
- resource_id: opaque id
- action: create|read|update|delete|invoke|authorize
- outcome: success|failure|denied|error
- http_method: optional (GET/POST) when applicable
- source_ip: CIDR or single IP (masked as needed)
- user_agent: free text
- policy_version: when action triggered by policy
- kv: optional free-form map (stringified JSON in NDJSON) with fields like prompt_hash, tokens_consumed, quantization_profile
- checksum: SHA256 of canonical event payload for tamper evidence
- sequence: monotonically increasing per-tenant counter (string or integer)

Notes on field handling for each SIEM: map these canonical names to their preferred field names (examples below). Some SIEMs have limits on nested objects; flatten kv into kv_prompt_hash, kv_tokens, etc., to avoid loss.

Mapping examples (summary):
- Splunk HEC: include _time (timestamp), host (tenant_id), sourcetype: redwood:audit, event: raw NDJSON. Recommended fields indexed: event_type, principal_id, resource_type, action, outcome, checksum. Use HEC batch size <= 10k events or 5MB.
- Datadog: send as JSON, set ddsource: redwood, service: redwood-audit, and use tags: tenant:<tenant_id>, env:<prod|staging>. Flatten kv to top-level fields to utilize facets.
- Sentinel (Log Analytics): use custom log table RedWoodAudit_CL with fields suffixed _s for strings where required. For example, RequestId_s, TenantId_s, EventType_s, Outcome_s. Use ingestion batching and ingestion_time in workspace for retention policies.

RBAC v2 considerations (export-time enrichment):
- We store role assignments internally in RBAC v2. Exports should include both the principal_id and the effective_role snapshot at event time (e.g., effective_role: admin/read-only/editor). This avoids relying on live graph for historical audits.
- For multi-tenant customers, provide config flag include_role_history=true to include role_assignment_id and role_change_timestamp in export when required by compliance.
- When customers integrate with their own IdP, we map IdP subject -> principal_id and add idp_provider field. If a customer requests opaque IDs only, we can pseudonymize principal_name but must keep principal_id for traceability.

Evidence automation hooks (how SIEM export fits):
- Use case: a regression test fails in production; evidence-automation should be able to reconstruct the end-to-end activity chain by linking request_id -> sequence -> cached prompt snapshot (if allowed) -> model output hash.
- Approach: store lightweight snapshots as references in audit events (kv.prompt_ref_id) that point to archived objects in Evidence Store. SIEM events should include the prompt_ref_id so security playbooks can retrieve the full artifact when authorized.
- Access control: retrieval of evidence store artifacts requires separate KMS-authenticated flow; DO NOT expose artifact contents in streaming export unless customer explicitly opts in.

Connector operational checklist (to run during setup):
1) Validate endpoint + certs: verify TLS and root CA chain; if mTLS required exchange certs and validate CN enforcement.
2) Schema agreement: share sample NDJSON of 100 events with customer. Confirm field names and masking rules.
3) Rate plan: agree on steady-state qps and burst tolerance. Configure batching windows (prefer 1s or 100ms for near-real-time).
4) Backpressure and retries: implement idempotent PUT semantics where possible; include request_id and sequence to dedupe. Retries: exponential backoff with jitter, cap at 5 retries before write-to-durable-fail-queue.
5) Monitoring alerts: failed delivery > 5% over 5m, queue growth > 10k events, checksum mismatch rate > 0.1% -> pager.
6) Data retention & disposal: confirm retention class and deletion procedure per tenant. For SFTP drops, confirm rotation and secure deletion schedule.

Sample customer onboarding template (questions we send to security teams):
- Which SIEM are you using (Splunk/Datadog/Sentinel/other)? Provide endpoint and ingestion method preference.
- TLS or mTLS required? Provide cert CN and expiry windows.
- Do you require PII masking on principal_name and source_ip? (yes/no) If yes, provide allowed pseudonymization style.
- Real-time (<5s) or batched (hourly) ingestion?
- Desired retention period (days).
- Required fields to index/alert on (e.g., outcome=denied, event_type=policy.change).
- RBAC snapshot included? (yes/no)
- Evidence artifacts allowed in export? (none/refs/inline when encrypted)
- On-call escalation for connector issues (name, pager, email)

Operational runbook excerpts (incident scenarios):
Scenario A - HEC returns 413 (payload too large):
- Action: reduce batch size, split current batch by event count and retry. If persistent, enable per-event fallback to write-to-sftp with note for later backfill.

Scenario B - consecutive 401 from Datadog tokens:
- Action: check token rotation schedule, try token refresh via customer-managed secret store, failover to secondary token if provided, notify customer and rollback to buffered storage.

Scenario C - sequence gap detected for tenant (missing sequence 102, 103):
- Action: mark sequence gap alert, try to locate events in local durable queue, rehydrate events to SIEM in order if available, annotate rehydrated events with rehydration=true and original_sequence. If events not available, produce a gap_event in SIEM that notes checksum and time ranges for forensic.

Privacy and compliance guardrails:
- Default export should redact response content for models flagged as "sensitive-output". Allow opt-in for full content export with signed BAAs and additional controls.
- PII fields: principal_name, email, message_text should be masked by default. We provide a regex-based mask with configurable exceptions.

Developer notes for connector implementers:
- Keep payload size under 5MB per HTTP request for maximum compatibility. Many proxies break above this.
- Prefer NDJSON (newline-delimited JSON) for batch uploads; each line must be a complete JSON object.
- Include HTTP header X-Redwood-Export-Version: 2024-09 and X-Redwood-Tenant: <tenant_id> for easier routing on customer side.
- Provide a /health and /metrics endpoint for the connector for customer network checks.

Open questions / items for SC/SE follow-up:
- Do customers want native event signing (we can sign events with a per-tenant signing key for tamper proofing)? Pros: better chain-of-custody. Cons: key management complexity.
- For Sentinel ingestion, confirm if customers prefer the Data Collector API or Azure Event Hubs for large-scale ingestion.
- Need standard mapping table for kv.* fields to top-level facets in Datadog - ticketed as JIRA SEC-1288.

Appendix - short sample event (NDJSON line):
{
  timestamp: 2024-09-17T18:22:03Z,
  event_type: model.invoke,
  request_id: 6d9f2a7a-9c8b-4f1a-b0f0-1a2b3c4d5e6f,
  tenant_id: org_7601,
  principal_type: service_account,
  principal_id: svc_42,
  principal_name: svc-ingest@acme.example,
  resource_type: model,
  resource_id: gpt-xxl-v1,
  action: invoke,
  outcome: success,
  kv_prompt_ref_id: pr_98123,
  kv_tokens_consumed: 412,
  checksum: e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4,
  sequence: 93012
}

If you want this converted into a concise customer-facing checklist PDF or a Splunk/Datadog/Sentinel field-mapping CSV, tell me which target and I'll produce that export-ready artifact.
